items.explanation: Senator Joseph McCarthy is best known for leading public investigations and accusations of communist infiltration in U.S. government and society. Choice B is wrong because McCarthy supported, not opposed, U.S. NATO commitments. Choice D is wrong because civil-rights legislation came primarily through the Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson administrations, not McCarthy's subcommittee. McCarthy's tactics defined the broader Second Red Scare phenomenon now called McCarthyism.

Desde su discurso del 9 de febrero de 1950 en Wheeling hasta las audiencias Ejército-McCarthy de 1954, acusó a cientos de funcionarios, intelectuales y artistas de deslealtad con poca o ninguna evidencia. La opción B es incorrecta porque McCarthy apoyó, no se opuso, a los compromisos de EE. UU. con la OTAN. La opción D es incorrecta porque la legislación de derechos civiles llegó principalmente a través de los gobiernos de Eisenhower, Kennedy y Johnson, no del subcomité de McCarthy. Las tácticas de McCarthy definieron el fenómeno más amplio del Segundo Susto Rojo, hoy llamado macartismo.

items.stem: During the Second Red Scare, McCarthyism damaged the careers of thousands of Americans. A political scientist argues that McCarthyism was more a symptom of institutional failure than of individual demagoguery. Which of the following pieces of evidence BEST supports this structural argument?
items.stemEs: Durante el Segundo Pánico Rojo, el macartismo arruinó las carreras de miles de estadounidenses. Un politólogo argumenta que el macartismo fue más un síntoma de fracaso institucional que de demagogia individual. ¿Cuál de las siguientes evidencias respalda MEJOR este argumento estructural?

choices.text: McCarthy's uniquely persuasive speaking style allowed him to intimidate even experienced politicians into public silence and cooperation
choices.textEs: El estilo oratorio personal de McCarthy era excepcionalmente persuasivo y le permitía intimidar incluso a políticos experimentados hasta el silencio.

choices.text: HUAC had generated anti-communist blacklists before McCarthy's rise, and Hoover's FBI supplied unverified accusations — showing multiple institutions enabled the Red Scare
choices.textEs: El HUAC ya realizaba audiencias anticomunistas y generaba listas negras antes del ascenso de McCarthy, y el FBI bajo Hoover le proporcionaba acusaciones no verificadas, demostrando que múltiples instituciones habilitaron el Pánico Rojo.

choices.text: Soviet espionage successes like the Rosenberg atomic spy case provided strong evidence that McCarthy's general concerns were entirely valid
choices.textEs: Los éxitos del espionaje soviético, incluido el robo de secretos nucleares por los Rosenberg, proporcionaron pruebas irrefutables de que las preocupaciones de McCarthy eran completamente válidas.

choices.text: American fear of nuclear annihilation made the public uniquely vulnerable to McCarthy's demagoguery in ways not seen before in U.S. politics
choices.textEs: El miedo generalizado del público americano a la aniquilación nuclear los hizo especialmente vulnerables a la manipulación de McCarthy de maneras que no habrían ocurrido en tiempos de paz.

items.explanation: McCarthyism was enabled by institutional failures: the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) had been conducting hearings and blacklists before McCarthy emerged; the FBI under Hoover actively supplied McCarthy with unverified information; and Congress, the press, and the legal system failed to challenge him effectively for years. This institutional complicity—not just McCarthy's personal charisma—explains the scope and duration of the Red Scare. McCarthy's eventual censure in 1954 illustrates that when institutions finally acted, the movement collapsed quickly.

Esta complicidad institucional —no solo el carisma personal de McCarthy— explica el alcance y la duración del Pánico Rojo.

items.stem: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of espionage and executed in 1953. Historians continue to debate whether their punishment was just. Considering the evidence available at the time of their trial versus evidence that emerged later, which conclusion is MOST defensible?

choices.text: Both Rosenbergs were clearly innocent victims of anti-communist hysteria, as Soviet archives have since confirmed that no American passed nuclear secrets to the USSR.
choices.textEs: Ambos Rosenberg eran claramente víctimas inocentes de la histeria anticomunista, ya que los archivos soviéticos han confirmado desde entonces que ningún estadounidense pasó secretos nucleares a la URSS.

choices.text: Both Rosenbergs were unambiguously guilty, and their execution was a proportionate response given the strategic damage caused by Soviet acquisition of nuclear technology.
choices.textEs: Ambos Rosenberg eran inequívocamente culpables, y su ejecución fue una respuesta proporcionada dado el daño estratégico causado por la adquisición soviética de tecnología nuclear.

choices.text: Later declassified evidence confirms Julius was a Soviet spy, but the case against Ethel relied on perjured testimony, suggesting her execution was disproportionate and shaped by Cold War political pressure.
choices.textEs: Evidencia desclasificada posterior confirma que Julius era un espía soviético, pero el caso contra Ethel se basó en testimonio perjuro, lo que sugiere que su ejecución fue desproporcionada y moldeada por la presión política de la Guerra Fría.

choices.text: The trial was entirely fair by the legal standards of the time, and later revelations about Soviet espionage fully vindicate every aspect of the prosecution's case.
choices.textEs: El juicio fue completamente justo según los estándares legales de la época, y las revelaciones posteriores sobre el espionaje soviético vindicaron plenamente todos los aspectos del caso de la acusación.

items.explanation: Declassified VENONA intercepts released in the 1990s confirmed Julius Rosenberg's role as a Soviet spy. However, the evidence against Ethel was far weaker—based largely on the testimony of her brother, David Greenglass, who later admitted he lied to protect his own wife. Historians now largely agree Julius was guilty of espionage, but that Ethel's execution was disproportionate given the thin evidence against her specifically, and that the trial reflected Cold War hysteria as much as evidence-based justice.
items.explanationEs: Los interceptos VENONA desclasificados en los años 90 confirmaron el papel de Julius Rosenberg como espía soviético. Sin embargo, la evidencia contra Ethel era mucho más débil, basada en gran medida en el testimonio de su hermano David Greenglass, quien posteriormente admitió haber mentido para proteger a su propia esposa. Los historiadores ahora coinciden en que Julius era culpable, pero que la ejecución de Ethel fue desproporcionada dada la escasa evidencia específica contra ella.

items.stem: Explain how McCarthyism and the Red Scare of the 1950s both protected and threatened American democracy. Provide specific evidence for each side of this tension.
items.stemEs: Explique cómo el macartismo y la Amenaza Roja de los 1950 tanto protegieron como amenazaron la democracia americana.
items.correctAnswer: Protection argument: Some Soviet espionage was real (Alger Hiss, Rosenbergs); vigilance against infiltration had legitimate national security basis. Threat argument: McCarthy's tactics violated due process, destroyed careers based on accusation alone, chilled free speech and political dissent, targeted innocent people, and used fear to consolidate political power. The greater threat to democracy came from McCarthyism itself — it demonstrated that fear could be weaponized to suppress democratic freedoms.
items.explanation: Real Soviet espionage cases such as Alger Hiss and the Rosenbergs gave anti-communism some legitimate national security basis, so a strong response should acknowledge why many Americans feared communist infiltration. A strong answer must also explain that McCarthy's accusations, blacklists, and loyalty investigations often ignored due process, ruined careers, and chilled free speech. The best responses use specific evidence on both sides and then judge whether protecting the nation ever justified methods that weakened democratic rights.
items.explanationEs: Los estudiantes deben analizar ambos lados de una tensión histórica con evidencia específica.

items.stem: Senator Joseph McCarthy made his first public claim of communist infiltration in the State Department in February 1950 — just months after the Soviet atomic test and the Chinese Communist revolution — and his accusations quickly resulted in the firing of experienced East Asia specialists. What does the timing and political impact of McCarthy's charges reveal about the relationship between foreign policy setbacks and domestic political culture?

choices.text: McCarthy's success demonstrates that American democratic institutions were fundamentally unprepared to resist demagogy during Cold War anxieties, since the executive and legislative branches failed to challenge his accusations despite the absence of corroborating evidence for his most sweeping claims.

The timing of McCarthy's rise reveals that anticommunism served as a tool for political entrepreneurs to pursue partisan objectives under cover of national security, with the substance of his claims mattering less than their instrumental value for attacking the Truman administration's foreign policy record.

The McCarthyite period demonstrates that citizens in democratic societies will consistently sacrifice civil liberties during national security crises, as the broad public support for McCarthy's investigations showed that most Americans prioritized security over the constitutional protections they theoretically endorsed.

Foreign policy setbacks created an environment of public anxiety in which McCarthy's charges could gain political traction regardless of their evidentiary basis, illustrating how genuine external security threats can be exploited to generate domestic political power through the systematic manipulation of fear rather than through accurate threat assessment.

items.explanation: The direct temporal connection between the Soviet atomic test, the Chinese Communist victory, and McCarthy's first accusations illustrates the mechanism: genuine foreign policy reversals created authentic public anxiety that McCarthy could exploit by offering a simple explanation — domestic betrayal — that was emotionally satisfying even if factually unsupported.

items.stem: Which best explains the lasting impact of McCarthyism on American political culture during the 1950s?

choices.text: McCarthyism permanently strengthened the authority of congressional committees to conduct unrestricted investigations of the executive branch.
McCarthyism demonstrated that public accusations of disloyalty, even without substantive evidence, could destroy careers and chill political dissent.
The Army-McCarthy hearings ultimately produced public demand for stronger due process protections that were codified in federal law.
McCarthyism led directly to legislation prohibiting political parties from advocating socialist or communist economic platforms.

items.explanation: The central legacy of McCarthyism was its demonstration that the political and social costs of being labeled disloyal — even falsely — were so severe that many Americans and institutions self-censored. This chilling effect on dissent is McCarthyism's most durable historical lesson.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from Senator Joseph McCarthy's speech to the Senate, June 14, 1951, Congressional Record — a U.S. government document available through the National Archives:

"How can we account for our present situation unless we believe that men high in this government are concerting to deliver us to disaster? This must be the product of a great conspiracy, a conspiracy on a scale so immense as to dwarf any previous such venture in the history of man... What is the objective of the great conspiracy? I think it is clear from what has occurred and is now occurring: to diminish the United States in world affairs, to weaken us militarily, to confuse our spirit with talk of surrender in the Far East and to impair our will to resist evil."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare (US.64), write a CER response that analyzes how McCarthy's tactics both reflected and intensified the ideological anxieties of the Cold War. Your response must assess the long-term damage McCarthyism inflicted on civil liberties and democratic institutions, and connect the Red Scare to the broader ideological conflict between the United States and the Soviet Union (US.59) that made such rhetoric politically powerful.
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento del discurso del Senador Joseph McCarthy ante el Senado, 14 de junio de 1951, Registro del Congreso — un documento del gobierno de EE. UU. disponible a través de los Archivos Nacionales:

"¿Cómo podemos explicar nuestra situación actual a menos que creamos que hombres con alto cargo en este gobierno están conspirando para entregarnos al desastre? Esto debe ser el producto de una gran conspiración, una conspiración de una escala tan inmensa que empequeñece cualquier empresa anterior de este tipo en la historia del hombre..."

Usando este fragmento y tu conocimiento del macartismo y la Segunda Caza de Brujas Roja (US.64), escribe una respuesta CER que analice cómo las tácticas de McCarthy reflejaron e intensificaron las ansiedades ideológicas de la Guerra Fría. Tu respuesta debe evaluar el daño a largo plazo que el macartismo infligió a las libertades civiles y las instituciones democráticas.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM — McCarthyism exploited the genuine anxieties produced by Cold War ideological conflict to create a domestic culture of suspicion that systematically violated civil liberties, ultimately undermining the very democratic institutions the U.S. claimed to be defending against Soviet communism. EVIDENCE — (1) McCarthy's accusation of State Department Communist infiltration (February 1950, Wheeling, WV) with numbers that shifted from 205 to 57 to 81 — demonstrating evidence-free accusations as political weapon; (2) HUAC investigations and Hollywood blacklist (hundreds of careers destroyed without due process); (3) Army-McCarthy Hearings (1954) and Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency?' moment; (4) Federal Employee Loyalty Program (Truman, 1947) as institutionalization of political surveillance; (5) Smith Act convictions of Communist Party leaders; (6) Senate censure of McCarthy (December 1954) as institutional self-correction. REASONING — McCarthy's effectiveness was rooted in the Cold War's ideological binary: in a world divided between freedom and communism, any accusation of communist sympathy was existentially threatening. The student should reason that McCarthyism was paradoxically self-defeating — its suppression of dissent, due process violations, and guilt-by-association tactics replicated the very authoritarian methods the U.S. opposed in the Soviet Union, revealing the tension between security imperatives and constitutional values.

items.explanation:

4 - Exemplary: Claim identifies the paradox of McCarthyism (defending democracy through anti-democratic means). Evidence includes at least three specific examples (Wheeling speech, HUAC, Army-McCarthy hearings, loyalty programs, Hollywood blacklist). Reasoning develops the Cold War ideological context that made McCarthyism viable AND the long-term institutional damage. CER fully integrated.
3 - Proficient: Clear claim about McCarthyism's damage to civil liberties. Two specific evidence points. Reasoning connects McCarthyism to Cold War anxiety but may not develop the paradox or institutional analysis.
2 - Developing: General claim about McCarthyism being bad or unjust. One specific evidence point. Reasoning is mostly descriptive.
1 - Beginning: Vague claim. Generic references to McCarthyism with no specific evidence. No analysis.
0 - No response or off-topic.

Murrow broadcast critique.

The Second Red Scare and McCarthyism (1947–1954) have been analyzed both as a rational response to genuine Cold War security threats and as a political hysteria that damaged American democracy. Using the CER framework, write an extended response that evaluates McCarthyism's causes, methods, and long-term consequences within the context of the broader Cold War. Your response should: (1) construct a thesis that takes a defensible position on whether McCarthyism was primarily a product of genuine security concerns, political opportunism, or systemic social anxieties; (2) analyze at least four specific cases, policies, or events that illustrate McCarthyism's methods and impact; and (3) evaluate the long-term consequences of McCarthyism for American civil liberties, political culture, and Cold War policy, synthesizing knowledge across US.59, US.60, US.63, and US.64.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — No se proporcionan fuentes. Basa tu respuesta en tu conocimiento de la historia de la Guerra Fría (US.59–US.70).

La Segunda Caza de Brujas Roja y el macartismo (1947–1954) han sido analizados tanto como una respuesta racional a amenazas reales de seguridad de la Guerra Fría como una histeria política que dañó la democracia estadounidense. Usando el marco CER, escribe una respuesta extendida que evalúe las causas, los métodos y las consecuencias a largo plazo del macartismo dentro del contexto más amplio de la Guerra Fría. Tu respuesta debe: (1) construir una tesis que tome una posición defendible sobre si el macartismo fue principalmente un producto de preocupaciones de seguridad genuinas, oportunismo político o ansiedades sociales sistémicas; (2) analizar al menos cuatro casos, políticas o eventos específicos; y (3) evaluar las consecuencias a largo plazo del macartismo.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) extended response would include: CLAIM — A precise, defensible thesis that synthesizes all three causal factors (e.g., 'McCarthyism emerged from the convergence of genuine but exaggerated security threats, deliberate political opportunism by McCarthy and HUAC, and deep social anxieties about rapid postwar change — but its most significant consequence was not its effect on Communist infiltration (minimal) but its chilling effect on democratic discourse, which paradoxically made the U.S. less democratic in its methods of defending democracy'). EVIDENCE across four cases/policies: (1) The genuine security context: Soviet atomic test (1949), Communist victory in China (1949), Rosenberg espionage case (1950), and Korean War — all created real anxiety that Soviet intelligence was winning; (2) McCarthy's specific methods: the Wheeling speech (Feb. 1950) with shifting numbers; 'lists' of Communists that were never released; guilt by association as investigative method; exploiting HUAC as platform; (3) HUAC and the Hollywood Blacklist — approximately 320 entertainment industry professionals blacklisted without due process; the 'naming names' dynamic that turned accusation into a loyalty performance; (4) Institutional responses: Federal Employee Loyalty Program (Truman, 1947); Smith Act prosecutions; Army-McCarthy Hearings (1954) and Senate censure as the democratic self-correction mechanism. REASONING — The student should reason that the genuine security threats were real but did not justify the methods: actual Soviet agents (Hiss, Rosenbergs) were caught by legitimate intelligence work, not by McCarthy's lists. The political opportunism dimension is crucial — McCarthy personally rose from obscurity to national prominence through accusation alone, demonstrating the political incentives that sustained the hysteria beyond any rational security calculus. SYNTHESIS — The response should connect McCarthyism's domestic effects (chilling of foreign policy dissent, US.60 and US.63) to the strategic limitations it imposed: the inability to recognize the Sino-Soviet split, the rigid bipolarity of U.S. Cold War thinking, and the domestic political costs of any policy that appeared 'soft on communism.'

items.stem: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited racial discrimination in public accommodations, employment, and federally funded programs. Given that many Southern states had maintained legally enforced segregation for nearly a century after the Fourteenth Amendment's passage, what does the Act's eventual passage most reveal about the conditions required for transformative civil rights legislation?
items.stemEs: La Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 prohibió la discriminación racial en los establecimientos públicos, el empleo y los programas financiados con fondos federales. Dado que muchos estados del Sur habían mantenido una segregación legalmente impuesta durante casi un siglo después de la aprobación de la Decimocuarta Enmienda, ¿qué revela más claramente la eventual aprobación de la Ley sobre las condiciones necesarias para la legislación transformadora en materia de derechos civiles?

choices.text: The Act demonstrated that moral argument alone can overcome entrenched racial hierarchies, as the movement's nonviolent discipline and the moral clarity of its witness ultimately convinced a sufficient congressional majority to act despite fierce Southern opposition.
choices.textEs: La Ley demostró que el argumento moral por sí solo puede superar las jerarquías raciales arraigadas, ya que la disciplina no violenta del movimiento y la claridad moral de su testimonio finalmente convencieron a una mayoría suficiente del Congreso de actuar a pesar de la feroz oposición del Sur.

choices.text: The Act's passage shows that economic modernization in the South had eroded the material foundation of segregation by creating a business class that recognized international competitiveness required abandoning racial discrimination, making economic development the primary structural driver of civil rights legislation.
choices.textEs: La aprobación de la Ley muestra que la modernización económica del Sur había erosionado la base material de la segregación al crear una clase empresarial que reconoció que la competitividad internacional requería abandonar la discriminación racial, haciendo del desarrollo económico el principal motor estructural de la legislación de derechos civiles.

choices.text: The Civil Rights Act passed primarily because of Lyndon Johnson's legislative mastery and his exploitation of the national emotional response to Kennedy's assassination, suggesting that individual political leadership and historically contingent events were more decisive than structural conditions in producing the legislation.
choices.textEs: La Ley de Derechos Civiles se aprobó principalmente gracias al dominio legislativo de Lyndon Johnson y su explotación de la respuesta emocional nacional al asesinato de Kennedy, lo que sugiere que el liderazgo político individual y los eventos históricamente contingentes fueron más decisivos que las condiciones estructurales para producir la legislación.

choices.text: The Act's passage required the convergence of sustained grassroots mobilization that disrupted segregation's daily functioning, television coverage that made white violence against nonviolent protesters politically costly to tolerate, and presidential leadership committed to legislative action — demonstrating that transformative civil rights legislation emerges from the alignment of movement pressure, public opinion shifts, and executive political
choices.textEs: La aprobación de la Ley requirió la convergencia de una movilización popular sostenida que perturbó el funcionamiento diario de la segregación, la cobertura televisiva que hizo políticamente costoso tolerar la violencia blanca contra los manifestantes no violentos, y el liderazgo presidencial comprometido con la acción legislativa —demostrando que la legislación transformadora de derechos civiles surge de la alineación de la presión del movimiento, los cambios en la opinión pública y la voluntad política ejecutiva.

items.explanation: The Civil Rights Act required multiple conditions aligned simultaneously: the civil rights movement had disrupted segregation's stability; television had transformed local white violence into national political liabilities; Cold War ideology made racial discrimination internationally embarrassing; and Johnson provided the executive commitment and legislative strategy to convert movement pressure into law.
items.explanationEs: La Ley de Derechos Civiles requirió que múltiples condiciones se alinearan simultáneamente: el movimiento de derechos civiles había perturbado la estabilidad de la segregación; la televisión había transformado la violencia blanca local en pasivos políticos nacionales; la ideología de la Guerra Fría hacía la discriminación racial internacionalmente vergonzosa; y Johnson aportó el compromiso ejecutivo y la estrategia legislativa para convertir la presión del movimiento en ley.
